title: The Vantablack feud
hook: One artist got exclusive rights to a super-black, and another banned him from pink.
peek: In 2016 the sculptor Anish Kapoor secured exclusive artistic rights to Vantablack, one of the darkest materials ever made. Fellow artist Stuart Semple hit back with a pink pigment anyone could buy, except Anish Kapoor.
lede: In 2014 the British firm Surrey NanoSystems unveiled Vantablack, a coating of tiny carbon tubes that absorbs about 99.96% of visible light. Shapes coated in it look like holes cut in the world. In 2016 the sculptor Anish Kapoor gained exclusive rights to use it in art, and many artists were furious.

bullets.text: Vantablack is not a paint. It is grown as a dense forest of carbon nanotubes, each far thinner than a hair. Light that enters bounces between them and almost none comes back out.
The artist Stuart Semple responded by selling a bright pigment he called the Pinkest Pink to everyone except Kapoor. Buyers had to confirm they were not Anish Kapoor or acting on his behalf.
Kapoor answered by posting a photo of his finger dipped in the pink on Instagram. Semple went on to make Black 2.0 and Black 3.0, very dark paints that anyone could buy.
Artists have tied themselves to colors before. Yves Klein registered the formula for his blue in 1960, though he never stopped others using ultramarine.
In 2019 MIT engineers reported a carbon nanotube coating that absorbed even more light. The artist Diemut Strebe used it to coat a large diamond, which nearly vanished into black.
The feud is the latest twist in a long story of colors made in labs, which began in earnest when a teenage William Perkin stumbled on mauve in 1856.
